lesson.title: The OSI Model: Seven Layers That Give Networking a Shared Vocabulary
lesson.summary: The OSI reference model is a seven layer framework for describing networking functions, giving engineers a common vocabulary for talking about layered architecture even though it is rarely implemented exactly as written.
lesson.body:
In the late 1970s and early 1980s, the International Organization for Standardization set out to describe, in a standardized and vendor neutral way, everything a layered network architecture needs to do. The result was the Open Systems Interconnection model, almost always called the OSI model, which breaks networking into exactly seven layers, from the physical transmission of bits at the bottom to the applications people actually use at the top: Physical, Data Link, Network, Transport, Session, Presentation, and Application.

Each layer has a specific, well defined job. The Physical layer deals with actual signals on wires, fiber, or radio. The Data Link layer organizes those raw bits into frames and handles addressing on a single local network segment. The Network layer handles addressing and routing across multiple interconnected networks. The Transport layer manages reliable, ordered delivery between two specific programs. The Session layer manages the setup, coordination, and teardown of a communication session between two systems. The Presentation layer handles translation, such as character encoding or encryption, so data is represented in a form both ends can understand. The Application layer is where the actual software, such as a web browser or an email client, interacts with the network.

It is important to be precise about what the OSI model is and is not. It was designed as a complete standard, with the intention that real protocols would be built to implement each of its seven layers exactly. In practice, that full seven layer implementation was never widely adopted commercially, the Internet instead grew up around the different, four layer TCP IP model covered in the next chapter. What did stick, and stick permanently, is the OSI model as a reference model, a shared vocabulary. When network engineers today talk about "a Layer 2 switch" or "a Layer 3 issue," they are using OSI's numbering even though the actual protocols running underneath, such as Ethernet and IP, were not designed strictly according to OSI's seven layer plan.

A worked example shows how this vocabulary gets used. Suppose a network technician is troubleshooting a computer that cannot reach a website. Saying "check the Physical layer" means checking whether the cable is plugged in and the link light is on. Saying "check the Data Link layer" means checking whether the correct hardware address is being used and the local switch sees the device. Saying "check the Network layer" means checking whether the computer has a valid IP address and can reach its router. This layer by layer troubleshooting process, moving up the stack one problem at a time, is a direct, practical benefit of having the OSI model's shared numbering and terminology, independent of whether every protocol in use maps perfectly onto all seven layers.

Because the OSI model builds so directly on the general idea of layered architecture covered previously, understanding it mainly means learning its specific seven names and job descriptions, which then serve as reference points for the physical, data link, and network layers explored in the chapters ahead.
